edits.why_correct: Refeeding syndrome occurs when nutrition is restarted after a period of starvation, causing insulin-driven shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium into cells. The highest risk lies with people who have had little or no intake for more than a few days alongside significant weight loss, especially with alcohol misuse, which also causes thiamine deficiency. He needs feeding started slowly with thiamine and close electrolyte monitoring, in line with NICE nutrition support guidance. Source: Nutrition support for adults: oral nutrition support, enteral tube feeding and parenteral nutrition (CG32), NICE, 2006, updated 2017.

edits.why_correct: Excess cortisol causes muscle protein breakdown and a myopathy that mainly affects the large proximal muscles of the hips and shoulders. This explains her difficulty raising her arms and standing from a low seat while her hand strength remains normal. The weakness usually improves once cortisol levels are brought under control. Source: Cushing's syndrome: symptoms, NHS website, 2025.

edits.why_wrong: A. Chvostek's sign is twitching of the facial muscles when the facial nerve is tapped. B. Brudzinski's sign is reflex flexion of the hips and knees when the neck is flexed, seen in meningism. C. Murphy's sign is arrest of inspiration on palpating the gallbladder. D. Babinski's sign is an extensor plantar response from an upper motor neurone lesion.
edits.why_correct: Inflating a cuff above systolic pressure causes ischaemia of the forearm nerves, which in hypocalcaemia triggers carpal spasm with wrist flexion and finger extension. This is Trousseau's sign. After thyroidectomy it most often reflects damage to or removal of the parathyroid glands, and her calcium should be checked urgently. Source: Emergency management of acute hypocalcaemia in adult patients, Society for Endocrinology, 2016.

edits.why_correct: A firm, diffuse, painless goitre with gradually developing primary hypothyroidism is the typical presentation of Hashimoto thyroiditis. Autoimmune lymphocytic infiltration of the gland causes the goitre and progressive loss of thyroid hormone production. Thyroid peroxidase antibodies are usually strongly positive, and treatment is with levothyroxine. Source: Thyroid disease: assessment and management (NG145), NICE, 2019, updated 2023; Underactive thyroid: causes, NHS website, 2025.

edits.why_correct: Weight loss despite a good appetite, heat intolerance and a fine tremor are classic features of thyrotoxicosis, which increases sympathetic sensitivity and atrial excitability and is a recognised cause of new atrial fibrillation, particularly in older people. Thyroid function is therefore part of the routine work-up of new atrial fibrillation, and treating the thyrotoxicosis often allows sinus rhythm to return. Source: Atrial fibrillation: causes, NHS website, 2025; Thyroid disease: assessment and management (NG145), NICE, 2019, updated 2023.

edits.why_correct: In a patient who is thyrotoxic with a nodule, the key question is whether the nodule itself is producing hormone. A radionuclide (technetium-99m pertechnetate or radioiodine) scan shows uptake, so a toxic adenoma appears as a 'hot' nodule with suppression of the rest of the gland. Hot nodules are very rarely malignant, which also guides whether further cytology is needed. Source: Thyroid disease: assessment and management (NG145), NICE, 2019, updated 2023.

Mammary duct ectasia is a benign condition, usually after the menopause, causing a thick yellow, green or brown discharge from several ducts, not milk. D. Gynaecomastia is enlargement of male breast tissue. E. Mastitis is inflammation of the breast with pain, redness and warmth.
edits.exam_trap: B, Mammary duct ectasia — it is a common benign cause of discharge from both breasts, but the discharge is thick and coloured rather than milky.
edits.why_correct: Galactorrhoea is the discharge of milk from the breast unrelated to pregnancy or breastfeeding. Bilateral milky discharge from several ducts is typical. It should prompt a pregnancy test, a medication review, a serum prolactin and thyroid function tests. Source: Primary care clinical referral criteria: nipple discharge and galactorrhoea, NHS Cornwall and Isles of Scilly, accessed 2026.

edits.why_correct: Many symptoms of thyrotoxicosis, including tremor, palpitations, sweating and anxiety, are driven by increased sensitivity to adrenergic stimulation. A non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol relieves these quickly while antithyroid drugs take several weeks to lower hormone levels. It is contraindicated in asthma, which she does not have. Source: Thyroid disease: assessment and management (NG145), NICE, 2019, updated 2023; Overactive thyroid: treatment, NHS website, 2023.

edits.why_correct: Rapid weight loss, thirst and polyuria with hyperglycaemia and ketonuria in a slim teenager indicate type 1 diabetes. This results from autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells, causing absolute insulin deficiency. Without insulin, fat is broken down to ketones, which is why ketonuria is present, and she needs same-day specialist referral. Source: Diabetes (type 1 and type 2) in children and young people: diagnosis and management (NG18), NICE, 2015, updated 2023.

edits.why_correct: Adrenergic symptoms a few hours after a carbohydrate-rich meal, relieved by eating and never seen when fasting, suggest reactive (postprandial) hypoglycaemia, thought to reflect an exaggerated or delayed insulin response after the initial post-meal rise in glucose. Before the label is accepted, a low glucose should be documented during a typical episode (Whipple's triad), for example with a supervised mixed-meal test. Source: Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycaemic disorders, Endocrine Society guideline 2009, summarised by the Association for Laboratory Medicine (UK), 2019.

edits.why_correct: Whipple's triad confirms clinically significant hypoglycaemia: symptoms consistent with hypoglycaemia, a low plasma glucose measured during those symptoms, and resolution of symptoms once glucose is raised. All three elements are needed before investigating causes such as insulinoma. Source: Evaluation and management of adult hypoglycaemic disorders, Endocrine Society guideline 2009, summarised by the Association for Laboratory Medicine (UK), 2019.

edits.stem:
A 76-year-old retired miner who still smokes is admitted under the medical team after a fortnight of constipation, drinking more than usual and episodes of muddled thinking. He has lost weight without trying over the past two months. His adjusted calcium is markedly raised and his parathyroid hormone is suppressed.

Which underlying cause is most likely?
edits.why_correct: A rapid onset of marked symptomatic hypercalcaemia, weight loss and smoking in an older adult, with a suppressed PTH, point to malignancy. Tumours raise calcium through PTH-related peptide (for example squamous cell lung cancer) or bone metastases and myeloma, and the suppressed PTH shows the parathyroids are not the cause. Source: Hypercalcaemia in adult patients in secondary care, NHS Scotland Right Decisions, 2022; Emergency management of acute hypercalcaemia in adult patients, Society for Endocrinology, 2016.
